Text | Yiying Hao

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

In 2018, the World Health Organization (WHO) published new Environmental Noise Guidelines for the European Region, which state clearly that environmental noise is a serious threat to human health and one of the leading public health problems.

With economic growth and ever-rising demand for convenient transport, airports have been springing up like mushrooms after rain. In Europe, new airports and airport expansions are getting closer and closer to residential areas. City airports and helipads, by the nature of their function, are embedded right in urban space. The conflict between the resulting aircraft noise, economic development and people’s health and quality of life is growing ever sharper.

The guidelines strongly recommend keeping aircraft noise below 45 dB(A) Lden over the whole day and below 40 dB(A) Lnight at night. These limits are lower than those for the road traffic noise we are used to, and lower than those for railway noise. So what makes aircraft noise different, and why are its limits so strict? How does it threaten our health? And what exactly is used to assess its impact? Let’s go through it.

1. Characteristics of aircraft noise

a. Aircraft noise is loud. The engines, the main noise source, can exceed 140 dB at take-off. How loud is 140 dB? At 120 dB, sound already hurts the ear. Traffic noise beside a busy road is usually around 70 dB, and 120 dB sounds 32 times as loud as 70 dB. And 140 dB can cause permanent hearing damage.

(For more on decibels, see our earlier article: What on earth is a decibel (dB), and why 1 + 1 ≠ 2)

Because aircraft noise is mostly broadband, it attenuates relatively slowly as it travels, and residents living around airports put up with loud aircraft noise, intermittent or continuous, every day. Take Manchester Airport, a medium-sized UK airport with two runways. According to 2016 data, nearly 50 households were exposed to aircraft noise above 75 dB every day, and as many as 150 to aircraft noise above 70 dB. More than 46,000 households were disturbed every day by aircraft noise above 55 dB. The area affected by aircraft noise reached 64 km².

A Qantas Boeing 747-400 passing close to houses at the boundary of London Heathrow Airport, England. (Source: Wikipedia)

b. Aircraft noise has complex sources

Aircraft noise comes from three sources:

1) Mechanical noise from the rotating parts of the engine, most pronounced when the fan blades reach supersonic speeds.

2) Aerodynamic noise from the airflow around the aircraft’s surfaces, especially in fast, low-altitude flight.

3) Noise from aircraft systems (cockpit and cabin pressurization and air-conditioning systems, and auxiliary power units).

Mechanical noise is the main source of aircraft noise, and aircraft with different types of propulsion generate noise in different ways. In propeller aircraft, for example, most of the noise comes from the propellers and aerodynamics. Helicopter noise is aerodynamic noise from the main and tail rotors plus mechanical noise from the main gearbox and the various drive trains. In jet aircraft, the engines account for most of the noise during take-off and climb, such as the buzzing produced when the fan blade tips go supersonic.

Source localization on a jet aircraft at different frequencies (www.aero.jaxa.jp)

Here is what several different types of aircraft sound like as they fly overhead:

Besides differences between aircraft types, the same type of aircraft produces sound of different level and character in different phases of operation. An aircraft in flight can be treated as a line source, and each operating phase has to be handled separately: for example, ground noise while taxiing before take-off, thrust noise while climbing, and noise in level flight. Ground noise during taxiing has to be broken down further into noise at the holding point and noise while taxiing, and the geographic data of the sources has to be modeled according to the layout of each airport’s runways. In addition, because aircraft noise is not equally loud in all directions, models must account for source directivity, and different types of aircraft have different directivity patterns.

c. Aircraft noise is hard to reduce

As mentioned above, aircraft noise sources are loud and mostly broadband, the sources are high up, and propagation through the atmosphere is hard to control, all of which make noise reduction very difficult. Existing measures include advances in aircraft technology, higher operating altitudes and shorter climb and descent phases, as well as a range of operational controls at airports and measures such as airport design, planning of the surrounding area and sound insulation of homes. Later articles in this series will look at these in detail.

2. The harm done by aircraft noise

a. Annoyance

The most direct harm done by aircraft noise is annoyance among residents. A large body of research has established the relationship between aircraft noise level and annoyance. The figure below, from the WHO Environmental Noise Guidelines, shows the relationship between aircraft noise level and annoyance. At 45 dB, 10% of residents report being highly annoyed, which is why the guidelines strongly recommend keeping aircraft noise below 45 dB(A) Lden over the whole day.

Environmental Noise Guidelines for the European Region

b. Sleep disturbance

Research shows that 11% of residents surveyed said that aircraft noise at 40 dB seriously disturbed their sleep. Although this proportion is already above the benchmark (3%), the guideline development group decided not to lower the night-time limit for aircraft noise any further, because there were no acoustic data supporting a lower value.

c. Beyond these direct disturbances and harms, the health of residents exposed to aircraft noise over long periods can also suffer to varying degrees. Aircraft noise increases the risk of cardiovascular disease (high blood pressure and stroke), for example, and causes cognitive impairment and hearing damage.

And yet in 2020, Year One of COVID, some of our friends in Europe and America even began to miss the days of flying, though presumably not the high decibels on board -_-

3. Computer-modeled aircraft noise metrics

a. Noise envelopes

In 2011, the UK Department for Transport put forward the concept of a “noise envelope” for aircraft noise assessment, prompted by the ever-growing noise impact of expanding large airports; the aim was to use the concept to gather views and suggestions on aircraft noise assessment from all sides. By 2013, the concept had taken shape in the Civil Aviation Authority’s Noise Envelopes (CAP1129), which also set out the principles of assessment for the first time. Three approaches could make up a noise envelope: limiting the number of flights and passenger throughput; limiting noise exposure, through noise quotas (by aircraft type), noise contour area, noise contour shape and noise level limits; and limiting noise impact, in terms of the population and households exposed, the number of people annoyed by aircraft noise during the day, and the number whose sleep is disturbed by it at night.

b. Computer-modeled aircraft noise metrics

In 2017, the UK Civil Aviation Authority issued a new edition of its airspace change design guidance, CAP1520, which explicitly lists a set of metrics for assessing aircraft noise. For daytime flight paths, the modeling must produce the 51 dB(A) Leq,16h contour and the population within it, N65 contours (the number of flights louder than 65 dB), and a WebTAG calculation of the economic impact of aircraft noise on annoyance and health. For night-time flight paths, it must produce the 45 dB(A) Lnight contour and the population within it, N60 contours (the number of flights louder than 60 dB), and a WebTAG calculation of the economic impact of aircraft noise on sleep disturbance and health. Additional metrics may include Lmax levels and before-and-after changes in noise contours.

Modeling these metrics requires a whole series of detailed inputs: airport geographic data, flight data, aircraft types, flight tracks, terrain and population data, and more. In later articles in this series, I will explain how these noise assessment metrics can be controlled and how noise impact can be reduced effectively.

About the author: Yiying Hao (PhD in architecture and former postdoctoral researcher, University of Sheffield) is a senior engineer at Bureau Veritas in Manchester. Research interests: acoustic environment assessment for major infrastructure, large-scale noise mapping, and soundscape design and assessment. Yiying has led or played a major role in research and implementation projects on aircraft noise assessment, policy revision and soundscape design for several international airports, including Heathrow, Manchester, Dublin and Manston.
